title: Phase 2: EEM Deployment
text:
MD  Mat Davis 

In this phase, we deploy the Event Endpoint Management (EEM) operator and instantiate the management cluster. The configuration must bridge the gap between the Kubernetes Service (ClusterIP) and the Ingress layer, ensuring traffic remains encrypted and OIDC authentication flows are correctly established. For complete configuration options, default values, and platform-specific mandates, please consult the official IBM Event Endpoint Management installation guide.

2.1 Configure Helm Repository
Before deploying the operator, add the IBM Helm repository to your local client.
# 1. Add the IBM Helm Repo
helm repo add ibm-helm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IBM/charts/master/repo/ibm-helm

# 2. Update to ensure you have the latest chart versions
helm repo update

# 3. Verify the chart is available (Target: 11.7.1+)
helm search repo ibm-eem-operator


2.2 Install the EEM Operator
The EEM Operator manages the lifecycle of the Manager, Gateway, and Portal components.
Step 1: Install Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)

Option A: Air-Gapped (Direct Download)Option B: Connected (Direct Install)


Target: Restricted / Production
If your cluster cannot reach the public Helm repositories directly, download the chart archive using curl and install it from the local file.
# 1. Download the chart archive
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IBM/charts/master/repo/ibm-helm/ibm-eem-operator-crd-11.7.1.tgz

# 2. Install from the local file
helm install eem-crds ./ibm-eem-operator-crd-11.7.1.tgz \
  --namespace ibm-eem \
  --create-namespace


Target: Sandbox / POC with Internet Access
If your environment has outbound internet access, install directly from the IBM Helm repository.
helm install eem-crds ibm-helm/ibm-eem-operator-crd \
  --namespace ibm-eem \
  --create-namespace \
  --version 11.7.1



Step 2: Install the Operator

Option A: Air-Gapped (Local Configuration)Option B: Connected (Direct Install)


Target: Restricted / Production
If pulling images from an internal Artifactory, you must download the chart, extract it, and modify the values.yaml file to point the operator to your local registry.
# 1. Download the chart archive
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IBM/charts/master/repo/ibm-helm/ibm-eem-operator-11.7.1.tgz

# 2. Extract the archive
tar -xzf ibm-eem-operator-11.7.1.tgz
Configure Local Registry Paths: Open ibm-eem-operator/values.yaml in your preferred text editor.

Locate the public and private repository blocks at the top of the file and replace the IBM registry URLs with your internal Artifactory path.
In the images block, replace the strict @sha256:... digests with the standard version tag (e.g., :11.7.1).
If your Artifactory is configured for anonymous access, clear the operatorImagePullSecret value so the cluster does not attempt to authenticate.

Example configuration using a local lab Artifactory:
public:
  repo: artifactory.gym.lan:8443
  path: docker-local/ibm-eventendpointmanagement/
private:
  repo: artifactory.gym.lan:8443
  path: docker-local/ibm-eventendpointmanagement/

images:
  operator: ibm-eventendpointmanagement-operator:11.7.1
  eemManager: eim-backend:11.7.1
  egw: ibm-eventendpointmanagement/egw:11.7.1
  tutorialegw: egw-tutorial:11.7.1

# Clear this value if your registry allows anonymous pulls
operatorImagePullSecret: ""
Install the Operator: Once your values are saved, run the install command against the local directory.
# 3. Install from the local extracted directory
helm install eem-operator ./ibm-eem-operator \
  --namespace ibm-eem


Target: Sandbox / POC with Internet Access
If your environment has outbound internet access, install directly from the IBM Helm repository.
helm install eem-operator ibm-helm/ibm-eem-operator \
  --namespace ibm-eem \
  --version 11.7.1









TipVerification



Verify the operator is running before proceeding.
kubectl get deploy ibm-eem-operator -n ibm-eem
# Expected: 1/1 READY




2.3 Create Security Assets
EEM requires several Kubernetes secrets to be pre-provisioned for OIDC authentication and TLS trust.

1. OIDC Client Secret
This secret contains the credentials for your Identity Provider (Keycloak).
# Replace 'your-client-secret' with the value from Keycloak
kubectl create secret generic oidc-client-secret \
  --namespace ibm-eem \
  --from-literal=client-id='eem-portal' \
  --from-literal=client-secret='your-client-secret'


2. OIDC Trust Secret (Self-Signed Only)
If your Keycloak instance uses a self-signed certificate (common in labs), you must export its CA cert and mount it into EEM.
# 1. Download the cert from the Keycloak endpoint
echo | openssl s_client \
  -showcerts \
  -servername keycloak.my-haproxy.gym.lan \
  -connect keycloak.my-haproxy.gym.lan:443 2>/dev/null | \
  openssl x509 -outform PEM > keycloak.pem

# 2. Create the trust secret
kubectl create secret generic keycloak-trust-secret \
  --namespace ibm-eem \
  --from-file=ca.crt=keycloak.pem



2.4 Deploy the EEM Instance
We use a Custom Resource (CR) to define the EEM instance. Select the configuration that matches your environment.

Option A: Production (Generic)Option B: Lab (Self-Signed)Option C: AWS EKS (Local Auth)


Use Case: Standard deployment with valid CA-signed certificates and OIDC authentication.
Create a file named eem-instance.yaml:
apiVersion: events.ibm.com/v1beta1
kind: EventEndpointManagement
metadata:
  name: eem-manager
  namespace: ibm-eem
spec:
  license:
    accept: true
    license: 'L-CYBH-K48BZQ'
    metric: VIRTUAL_PROCESSOR_CORE
    use: EventAutomationProduction
  manager:
    endpoints:
      - name: ui
        host: eem-portal.corp
        annotations:
          # SSL Passthrough is NOT needed here; ALB TLS termination is fully supported.
          external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl: "300"
          kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "alb"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: "internal"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: "ip"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-protocol: "HTTPS"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/subnets: "subnet-xxxx, subnet-yyyy, subnet-zzzz"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/security-groups: "eks-lab-001-eks_worker_sg, eks-lab-001-eks_cluster_sg"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/tags: "Name=eem-lab-alb,tfc-after-hours=middleware-support,tfc-application-group=event-streaming,tfc-business-application-name=event-automation,tfc-business-application-code=app12,tfc-business-application-id=appid-00000000,tfc-business-cost-center=00000-0000,tfc-business-groupname=g-role-devops,tfc-created-by=engineering,tfc-technical-environment=lab,tfc-technical-supported-by=support@example.com"
      - name: gateway
        host: eem-gateway.corp
        annotations:
          # SSL Passthrough is NOT needed here; ALB TLS termination is fully supported.
          external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl: "300"
          kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "alb"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: "internal"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: "ip"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-protocol: "HTTPS"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/subnets: "subnet-xxxx, subnet-yyyy, subnet-zzzz"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/security-groups: "eks-lab-001-eks_worker_sg, eks-lab-001-eks_cluster_sg"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/tags: "Name=eem-lab-alb,tfc-after-hours=middleware-support,tfc-application-group=event-streaming,tfc-business-application-name=event-automation,tfc-business-application-code=app12,tfc-business-application-id=appid-00000000,tfc-business-cost-center=00000-0000,tfc-business-groupname=g-role-devops,tfc-created-by=engineering,tfc-technical-environment=lab,tfc-technical-supported-by=support@example.com"
      - name: admin
        host: eem-admin.corp
        annotations:
          # SSL Passthrough is NOT needed here; ALB TLS termination is fully supported.
          external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl: "300"
          kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "alb"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: "internal"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: "ip"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-protocol: "HTTPS"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/subnets: "subnet-xxxx, subnet-yyyy, subnet-zzzz"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/security-groups: "eks-lab-001-eks_worker_sg, eks-lab-001-eks_cluster_sg"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/tags: "Name=eem-lab-alb,tfc-after-hours=middleware-support,tfc-application-group=event-streaming,tfc-business-application-name=event-automation,tfc-business-application-code=app12,tfc-business-application-id=appid-00000000,tfc-business-cost-center=00000-0000,tfc-business-groupname=g-role-devops,tfc-created-by=engineering,tfc-technical-environment=lab,tfc-technical-supported-by=support@example.com"
      - name: server
        host: eem.server.corp
        annotations:
          # SSL Passthrough is NOT needed here; ALB TLS termination is fully supported.
          external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl: "300"
          kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "alb"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: "internal"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: "ip"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-protocol: "HTTPS"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "HTTPS"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/subnets: "subnet-xxxx, subnet-yyyy, subnet-zzzz"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/security-groups: "eks-lab-001-eks_worker_sg, eks-lab-001-eks_cluster_sg"
          alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/tags: "Name=eem-lab-alb,tfc-after-hours=middleware-support,tfc-application-group=event-streaming,tfc-business-application-name=event-automation,tfc-business-application-code=app12,tfc-business-application-id=appid-00000000,tfc-business-cost-center=00000-0000,tfc-business-groupname=g-role-devops,tfc-created-by=engineering,tfc-technical-environment=lab,tfc-technical-supported-by=support@example.com"
    authConfig:
      authType: OIDC
      oidcConfig:
        clientIDKey: client-id
        clientSecretKey: client-secret
        discovery: true
        secretName: oidc-client-secret
        site: 'https://keycloak.corp/realms/ibm-eem'
    # Mount the custom CA cert to trust Keycloak
    tls:
      trustedCertificates:
        - certificate: ca.crt
          secretName: keycloak-trust-secret
    storage:
      storageClassName: gp2
      type: persistent-claim
Apply the Configuration:
kubectl apply -f eem-instance.yaml

NoteStartup Time



The Operator will now provision the EEM Manager pod.
You can watch the pods spin up with: kubectl get pods -n ibm-eem -w
To monitor the actual readiness status of the deployment, watch the Custom Resource: kubectl get eventendpointmanagement eem-manager -n ibm-eem -w




2.5 Configure User Roles
When deploying your EEM instance, you must grant initial access to the system. The configuration depends entirely on your chosen authentication method.

Option A: OIDC Auth (UUID Mapping)Option B: Local Auth (Credentials & Mapping)


Use Case: External Identity Provider (Keycloak, Auth0, etc.)
By default, an OIDC user has no permissions upon first login. You must map the Identity Provider’s user subject (UUID) directly to the EEM roles.
1. Create the Mapping File: Create a file named myroles.json and replace the id below with your Keycloak User UUID.
{
  "mappings": [
    {
      "id": "130ea2d9-e60c-4f28-8499-386ecda2d825",
      "roles": [
        "admin",
        "author"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
2. Patch the Roles Secret: Inject this JSON directly into the user-roles secret managed by the operator.
kubectl patch secret eem-manager-ibm-eem-user-roles \
  --namespace ibm-eem \
  --type='json' \
  -p="[{\"op\" : \"replace\" ,\"path\" : \"/data/user-mapping.json\" ,\"value\" : \"$(cat myroles.json | base64 -w 0)\"}]"


Use Case: Built-in Local Directory
For local authentication, you must first define the user credentials, and then map that new user ID to the appropriate roles.
1. Create the Credentials File: Create a file named myusers.json with your desired administrator credentials.
{
    "users": [
        {
            "username": "eemadmin",
            "password": "Password1$"
        }
    ]
}
2. Patch the Credentials Secret: Inject the user definition into the credentials secret.
kubectl patch secret eem-manager-ibm-eem-user-credentials \
  --namespace ibm-eem \
  --type='json' \
  -p="[{\"op\" : \"replace\" ,\"path\" : \"/data/user-credentials.json\" ,\"value\" : \"$(cat myusers.json | base64 -w 0)\"}]"
3. Create the Mapping File: Create a file named myroles.json mapping your new username to the administrative roles.
{
  "mappings": [
    {
      "id": "eemadmin",
      "roles": [
        "admin",
        "author"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
4. Patch the Roles Secret: Inject the mapping JSON into the user-roles secret.
kubectl patch secret eem-manager-ibm-eem-user-roles \
  --namespace ibm-eem \
  --type='json' \
  -p="[{\"op\" : \"replace\" ,\"path\" : \"/data/user-mapping.json\" ,\"value\" : \"$(cat myroles.json | base64 -w 0)\"}]"









TipVerification



Navigate to your configured UI host (e.g., https://eem-portal.gym.lan or https://portal.eem.corp). Log in with your Keycloak or Local credentials. You should see the Administration and Manage menu items, confirming that the role mapping was successful.
Note: The role mapping might take a few minutes to propagate. If you see an “Unauthorized” message, wait a moment and refresh.

title: Phase 1: Foundation & Prerequisite Configuration
text:
MD  Mat Davis 

Before deploying the IBM Event Endpoint Management (EEM) operator, the infrastructure foundation must be secured. This phase covers provisioning the certificate manager, establishing the ingress layer, and configuring the external Identity Provider (IdP).

1.0 Create Namespace
Create the dedicated namespace for the EEM deployment. It is recommended to set your current context to this namespace to simplify subsequent commands.
# 1. Create the namespace
kubectl create namespace ibm-eem

# 2. Set as current context (Optional but recommended)
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=ibm-eem


1.1 Certificate Manager
EEM relies heavily on Cert-Manager for internal mTLS communication between the Manager, Gateway, and Portal components.

Option A: Production (Generic)Option B: Lab (Install)


On standard Kubernetes platforms, utilize an existing Certificate Manager installation.
Requirements:

Version: v1.12+ recommended.

APIs: Must support Issuer.cert-manager.io/v1 and Certificate.cert-manager.io/v1 GroupVersionKinds (GVK).

Alternative: If Cert-Manager is not allowed, you must manually create certificates for all components and provide them via Kubernetes secrets (complex).



For lab environments (e.g., k3s) where Cert-Manager is not yet present, install it via Helm.
# 1. Add the Jetstack repository
helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io
helm repo update

# 2. Install Cert-Manager
helm install \
  cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \
  --version v1.19.2 \
  --namespace cert-manager \
  --create-namespace \
  --set crds.enabled=true





1.2 Ingress Configuration
The Ingress Controller is the entry point for both API traffic (Gateway) and User traffic (Portal/Manager). The Gateway specifically requires SSL Passthrough to handle raw mTLS handshakes directly from Kafka clients.

Option A: Production (AWS EKS)Option B: Lab (Nginx)


Target: AWS EKS utilizing the AWS Load Balancer Controller.
In EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller provisions Application Load Balancers (ALBs) for Ingress resources and Network Load Balancers (NLBs) for Service resources. Because ALBs do not support SSL passthrough, routing for IBM Event Endpoint Management (EEM) components must be handled as follows:

EEM Manager (UI and APIs): The ingresses related directly to the EEM manager, which include the UI and other API endpoints, exclusively use HTTP/HTTPS. For these components, an Ingress generating an AWS ALB can be used and is fully supported.
Gateway Groups: When gateway groups are defined, an NLB with SSL passthrough is needed. This will require defining a Kubernetes Service (type LoadBalancer) with the appropriate AWS annotations when the gateway is deployed so that the proper NLB path is created. Even though the gateway deployment will also define an Ingress that might generate an ALB path, that specific ALB path can be ignored.



Install the Nginx Ingress Controller using Helm. The publishService flag is crucial for ensuring the LoadBalancer IP is correctly populated in Ingress statuses.
# 1. Add the Nginx repository
helm repo add ingress-nginx [https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx](https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx)
helm repo update

# 2. Install the Controller
helm install nginx-ingress ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx \
  --create-namespace \
  --set controller.kind=DaemonSet \
  --set controller.service.type=LoadBalancer \
  --set controller.publishService.enabled=true \
  --set controller.extraArgs.enable-ssl-passthrough=true \
  --set controller.allowSnippetAnnotations=true





1.3 DNS & Networking
Ensure your Identity Provider (Keycloak) and EEM endpoints are resolvable.

Requirement: The OIDC provider (e.g., keycloak.eem.gym.lan) must be accessible via DNS from inside the cluster pods.
Lab Setup: Use a wildcard DNS entry or edit your /etc/hosts file to point the desired hostname to the IP address of your ingress controller.







TipCoreDNS Caching



If you make changes at the networking level (like /etc/hosts on the nodes) and pods do not pick it up, reboot CoreDNS to flush the cache.
kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment coredns




1.4 Identity Provider (Keycloak)
EEM does not manage users internally; it requires an OIDC-compliant Identity Provider. Follow these steps to configure Keycloak for the lab.
A. Realm & Client Setup

Log in: Access Keycloak (e.g., admin/admin) and create a new realm called ibm-eem.
Create Client: Go to Clients > Create Client.

Client type: OpenID Connect
Client ID: eem-portal
Name: IBM Event Endpoint Management
Click Next.

Capability Config:

Client authentication: On (This enables “Confidential” access type).
Authorization: Off (EEM handles authorization mapping).
Authentication flow: Select Standard flow and Direct access grants.
Click Next.

Login Settings:

Root URL: (Leave blank)
Home URL: https://eem-portal.gym.lan
Valid redirect URIs: https://eem-portal.gym.lan/*

Note: The wildcard * is recommended for labs to cover various callback paths (e.g., /callback, /auth/callback).

Web origins: +
Click Save.

Capture Credentials:

Go to the Credentials tab.
Copy the Client Secret. You will need this for the EEM installation phase.


B. User Creation

Create User: Go to Users > Add user.

Username: admin-user
Email: admin@example.com (Crucial: Toggle Email Verified to On).
First Name: John
Last Name: Doe
Click Create.

Set Password:

Go to the Credentials tab.
Click Set password.
Password: password
Temporary: Toggle to Off (Prevents forced reset on first login).
Click Save.




1.5 Create Image Pull Secret
You must provide credentials to pull the IBM container images.

Option A: Private Registry (Air-Gapped)Option B: IBM Registry (Lab)


Target: Restricted / Production
If pulling from an internal Artifactory that requires authentication:
kubectl create secret docker-registry ibm-entitlement-key \
  --docker-server=artifactory.internal.corp \
  --docker-username=<SERVICE_ACCOUNT> \
  --docker-password=<TOKEN> \
  -n ibm-eem






ImportantAnonymous Artifactory Access



If your internal Artifactory is configured for anonymous pulls, and you plan to manually update the Helm values.yaml to point to this local registry, do not create this secret.
Creating a dummy ibm-entitlement-key secret when anonymous access is allowed will force the cluster to attempt authentication, which will fail and result in ImagePullBackOff errors.




Target: Sandbox / POC with Internet Access
Create a secret using your IBM Entitlement Key.
# 1. Get your key from [https://myibm.ibm.com/products-services/containerlibrary](https://myibm.ibm.com/products-services/containerlibrary)
# 2. Create the secret
kubectl create secret docker-registry ibm-entitlement-key \
  --docker-server=cp.icr.io \
  --docker-username=cp \
  --docker-password=<YOUR_IBM_ENTITLEMENT_KEY> \
  --docker-email=user@example.com \
  -n ibm-eem

title: Event Endpoint Management on EKS
text:
The Why
Enterprises are rapidly adopting Event-Driven Architectures (EDA) to power real-time customer experiences, but their operational maturity can lag behind their REST API ecosystems. While organizations have established rigorous governance, security, and discovery patterns for synchronous APIs (using tools like API-C), their Kafka environments often resemble “wild west” infrastructure.
This disparity creates a critical business risk: critical data streams are exposed without standardized security, discoverability is limited, and onboarding new consumers requires manual, ticket-based friction. This solution bridges that gap by deploying IBM Event Endpoint Management (EEM) to treat Events as first-class APIs.

Problem Details
The implementation of Event Management in a secure, cloud-native environment (AWS EKS) presents specific technical and process challenges:

The “Shadow Kafka” Problem: Developers cannot discover existing topics, leading to duplicated data streams and lack of reuse. There is no central catalog (portal) for event interfaces.
Inconsistent Security Posture: Kafka authentication is often handled via static credentials (SASL/SCRAM) or mTLS certificates that are difficult to rotate. There is a need to federate access using corporate Identity Providers (OIDC).
Consumption Friction: Onboarding a new application to a topic requires manual infrastructure changes (ACLs, firewall rules), slowing down innovation cycles.
Deployment Complexity: Deploying the EEM Gateway and Manager on EKS requires navigating complex ingress patterns, including AWS Network Load Balancers (NLB), Ingress Controllers, and strictly enforcing TLS/SSL requirements using enterprise CAs.



Additional Context
Environment & Constraints

Platform: AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS).

Kubernetes Version: Kubernetes platforms that support the Red Hat Universal Base Images (UBI) containers, versions 1.27 to 1.33.

Software Version: IBM EEM 11.7.1 (Helm Chart 11.7.1).
Identity Provider: OpenID Connect (e.g. Keycloak).
Ingress Controller: NGINX or similiar with SSL Passthrough.
Certificate Management: cert-manager v1.19.2 or similiar.

title: Deployment Readiness
text:
MD
Successful deployment of IBM Event Endpoint Management (EEM) into a cloud-native EKS environment requires specific infrastructure pillars to be established prior to installation. This section outlines the necessary tooling, ingress strategies, and identity configurations required to support the solution’s Kafka-Native architecture.
For a complete list of supported platforms and versions, please refer to the official Support Matrix.

title: Deployment Readiness
text:
Prerequisite Checklist
Before initiating the deployment pipeline, ensure the following prerequisites are met.

1. Workstation & Tooling
The automation bastion or engineer’s workstation requires connectivity to the target EKS cluster and the following CLI tools:

Helm 3 (v3.10+ recommended) for chart management.
Kubectl configured with the correct context.
OpenSSL for certificate verification and troubleshooting.
Skopeo (Optional): Recommended for mirroring images if the cluster is air-gapped.







TipHelm 3 install on Linux (RHEL 8):



curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash








TipSkopeo install on Linux (RHEL 8):



sudo dnf -y install skopeo




2. Ingress and Load Balancer Strategy
The EEM components require a split load balancing strategy to handle standard web traffic and the specialized Kafka protocol correctly. While standard TLS termination works perfectly for the Manager and UI, the Event Gateway requires direct TCP access to facilitate SSL passthrough for client certificate verification.
Requirement: Split AWS Load Balancers or SSL Passthrough
To accommodate these distinct routing needs, the cluster must be configured using one of the following approaches:

EEM Manager (ALB): The UI and API endpoints exclusively use HTTP/HTTPS. These are fully supported by standard Kubernetes Ingress resources backed by an AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB).
Event Gateway (NLB): When gateway groups are defined, SSL passthrough is mandatory. Because ALBs do not support this feature, you must deploy a Kubernetes Service (type LoadBalancer) configured to provision an AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB). The gateway will also automatically generate an Ingress resource, but the resulting ALB path can be ignored.
In-Cluster Controller Option: If you have the option to deploy a dedicated in-cluster ingress controller rather than relying entirely on AWS native routing, this is an option. Ensure the controller is exposed via a Layer 4 NLB and is configured to allow SSL passthrough.



3. Identity Provider (OIDC)
EEM delegates all user authentication to an external Identity Provider (IdP). A dedicated OpenID Connect (OIDC) client must be provisioned prior to installation.
Required Client Settings:

Client Type: Confidential (Must have a Client Secret).
Grant Types: Authorization Code, Refresh Token.
Redirect URIs: The IdP must whitelist the following callback patterns (replace *.eem.corp with your ingress domain):

https://manager.eem.corp/*
https://portal.eem.corp/*
https://gateway.eem.corp/*








NoteSelf-Signed IdP Certificates



If your OIDC provider (e.g., Keycloak) utilizes a self-signed certificate or a private CA, you must export the CA certificate. This file will be mounted into the EEM Manager and Gateway pods via the trustedCertificates configuration to prevent SSL handshake failures during the discovery phase.




4. Supply Chain (Image Mirroring)
The target environment prohibits direct access to public registries (cp.icr.io, icr.io). All container images must be staged in the internal trusted registry (e.g., Artifactory).






NoteIBM entitlement key



You will need an IBM entitlement key to mirror the images or install without mirroring. This can be obtained here.


Enterprise Pipeline Integration If the organization utilizes a centralized image ingestion process, please configure the pipeline to pull from both the IBM Entitled Registry and the IBM Open Registry.

Source Registries: cp.icr.io, icr.io
Source Namespaces: cp/ibm-eventendpointmanagement, cpopen/ibm-eventendpointmanagement, cpopen

Core Images:







Component
Image Path




Manager/Backend
cp.icr.io/cp/ibm-eventendpointmanagement/eim-backend


Operator
icr.io/cpopen/ibm-eventendpointmanagement-operator


Gateway
icr.io/cpopen/ibm-eventendpointmanagement/egw


Gateway Tutorial
icr.io/cpopen/ibm-eventendpointmanagement/egw-tutorial









TipFinding Exact Tags and Digests



Because IBM utilizes sha256 digests rather than standard version tags to guarantee image immutability, guessing tags or using skopeo list-tags can lead to manifest unknown errors (especially with single-architecture vs. multi-architecture index files).
The most reliable way to get the exact paths and digests for your specific deployment is to extract them directly from the Helm chart:
# 1. Pull and unpack the specific version of the chart
helm pull ibm-helm/ibm-eem-operator --version <VERSION> --untar

# 2. Extract every image reference and digest used by the operator
helm template dummy-release ./ibm-eem-operator | grep -iE 'image:|value:.*icr\.io' | sort -u
Use the output from this command to feed your mirroring tools (like skopeo copy), appending --preserve-digests to ensure the hashes remain identical in your local registry.




5. Cluster Services (Cert-Manager)
EEM has a hard dependency on Cert-Manager for managing internal TLS certificates between its microservices.
Requirements: Use a certificate manager installation, for example cert-manager, that supports Issuer.cert-manager.io/v1 and Certificate.cert-manager.io/v1 GroupVersionKind (GVK), or create certificates manually and provide them to Event Endpoint Management by using Kubernetes secrets.






TipLab & Sandbox Setup



If you are attempting to reproduce this environment in a local lab (e.g., k3s) where the API server cannot reach the webhook due to firewall restrictions, consider installing Cert-Manager with hostNetwork: true to bypass the CNI routing layer.




6. Storage Requirements
The EEM Manager and Portal require persistent storage for their configuration databases.

Storage Class: A valid ReadWriteOnce (RWO) storage class must be available (e.g., gp3 on EKS or local-path on K3s).
Capacity:

Manager: Minimum 10Gi recommended.
Portal: Minimum 5Gi recommended.

title: Troubleshooting & Diagnostics
section: Enabling Debug Logging in the EEM Manager
text:
Enabling Debug Logging in the EEM Manager
To get more visibility into UI parsing and backend validation errors, you can dynamically enable debug logging for the core IBM EEM packages without restarting the manager pod.
1. Apply the Trace Specification Patch Assuming your instance is named eem-manager, run the following command to inject the trace specification:
kubectl patch eventendpointmanagement eem-manager -n ibm-eem --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"manager":{"traceSpec":"com.ibm.ei:debug"}}}'
2. Verify the Configuration Tail the manager logs to confirm the configuration was picked up dynamically:
kubectl logs -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=eem-manager -n ibm-eem -c manager -f
You should see a confirmation message similar to this:
INFO  NULL com.ibm.ei.core.config.TraceSpecConfig - [applyLoggers:69] Setting trace specification from spec variable traceSpec: com.ibm.ei:debug

title: Phase 3: Gateway Deployment
text:
MD  Mat Davis 

With the EEM Manager and Gateway pods running, the next phase is establishing the data plane. The Gateway requires a backend Kafka cluster to route traffic to, and a Layer 4 network path to accept incoming mTLS/TLS client connections.

3.1 Backend Kafka Provisioning
The EEM Gateway acts as a secure proxy and requires a target Kafka cluster to manage.

Option A: Production (Bring Your Own Kafka)Option B: Lab (Test Broker)


Use Case: Connecting to an existing enterprise Kafka environment (e.g., AWS MSK, Confluent Cloud, or IBM Event Streams).
Ensure you have the following information from your Kafka administrators:
* Bootstrap server addresses.
* TLS certificates (if using secure connections).
* Authentication credentials (SCRAM, mTLS, or plain).


Use Case: Spinning up a temporary, lightweight Kafka broker in your k3s environment to validate Gateway routing with secure SSL connections (but without the complexity of Mutual TLS).
We can deploy a single-node Kafka instance using the Bitnami Helm chart, secured by a local Certificate Authority.
1. Generate the Local Certificates First, create the SSL certificates to secure the broker traffic:
# Create the Certificate Authority
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -days 365 -nodes -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt -subj "/CN=Kafka-Lab-CA"

# Create the Server Private Key and CSR
openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout server.key -out server.csr -subj "/CN=test-kafka.kafka-lab.svc.cluster.local"

# Define the Subject Alternative Names (SANs) for internal DNS
echo "subjectAltName=DNS:test-kafka.kafka-lab.svc.cluster.local,DNS:test-kafka.kafka-lab.svc,DNS:localhost" > extfile.cnf

# Sign the Server Certificate
openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out server.crt -days 365 -extfile extfile.cnf

# Load the certificates into a Kubernetes Secret
kubectl create namespace kafka-lab
kubectl create secret generic kafka-server-certs -n kafka-lab \
  --from-file=tls.crt=server.crt \
  --from-file=tls.key=server.key \
  --from-file=ca.crt=ca.crt
2. Deploy the Secure Broker Now, deploy the broker using the secret we just created. We explicitly set tls.clientAuth=none to enforce one-way SSL, bypassing the Mutual TLS (mTLS) requirement.
# Add the Bitnami repository
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update

# Install the secure Kafka cluster
helm install test-kafka bitnami/kafka \
  --namespace kafka-lab \
  --set replicaCount=1 \
  --set zookeeper.enabled=false \
  --set kraft.enabled=true \
  --set listeners.client.protocol=SSL \
  --set tls.enabled=true \
  --set tls.type=pem \
  --set tls.existingSecret=kafka-server-certs \
  --set listeners.client.sslClientAuth=none \
  --set image.repository=bitnamilegacy/kafka
Note: This creates a secure broker at test-kafka.kafka-lab.svc.cluster.local:9092 that encrypts traffic but does not require clients to present their own certificates.
3. Create the Backend Topic Because the broker is now expecting secure connections, we must pass a configuration file to the Kafka script so it knows to use SSL when connecting to create the topic.
Run this command to dynamically generate the client configuration inside the pod and create a topic named test-topic:
TRUST_PASS=$(kubectl get secret test-kafka-tls-passwords -n kafka-lab -o jsonpath='{.data.truststore-password}' | base64 -d) && \
kubectl exec -it test-kafka-controller-0 -n kafka-lab -- bash -c " \
  echo -e \"security.protocol=SSL
ssl.truststore.location=/opt/bitnami/kafka/config/certs/kafka.truststore.jks
ssl.truststore.password=$TRUST_PASS
ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm=\" > /tmp/client.properties && \
  kafka-topics.sh \
  --create \
  --bootstrap-server test-kafka.kafka-lab.svc.cluster.local:9092 \
  --topic test-topic \
  --partitions 1 \
  --replication-factor 1 \
  --command-config /tmp/client.properties"





3.2 Connect the Backend Kafka Cluster
Once the Gateway is connected, you must tell it where to route the Kafka traffic.

Option A: Production (Enterprise Kafka)Option B: Lab (Bitnami Test Broker)


Use Case: Connecting to AWS MSK, Confluent, or Event Streams.

Navigate to the Clusters page in the EEM UI.

Click Add cluster.
Enter a name (e.g., test-kafka-cluster).

Enter the DNS name and port for the bootstrap server: kafka.corp:443.

If certificates are set up for the Kafka broker, an error will display saying “Multiple certificates are not trusted”. Click “Accept all certificates”. Click Next.
On the Credentials screen, enter any client authentication needed. Click create to finish adding the cluster.



Use Case: Connecting to the plaintext Bitnami broker we spun up in the kafka-lab namespace.

Navigate to the Clusters page in the EEM UI.

Click Add cluster.

Enter a name (e.g., test-kafka-cluster).

Enter the internal Kubernetes DNS name for the bootstrap server: test-kafka.kafka-lab.svc.cluster.local:9092.

If certificates are set up for the Kafka cluster, you will be prompted to accept the certificates. Click Next.
On the Credentials screen, since we configured the broker for one-way SSL without client authentication. Click create to finish adding the cluster.










NotePending Validation Status



After adding the cluster, you will notice its state is listed as Pending validation. This is expected! The EEM Manager is simply “waiting for a gateway group to report a validation status.” Because the Manager itself does not connect directly to the broker for data traffic, the connection cannot be actively tested until we register a Gateway and link it to this cluster in the upcoming steps.




3.3 Register the Gateway in the EEM UI
Now that the infrastructure is ready, we need to register the Gateway with the Manager. This process generates a Custom Resource (CR) YAML file containing the cryptographic trust and connection details required for the two components to communicate.
1. Generate the Gateway YAML:

Log into the EEM Manager UI.

Navigate to the Gateways page from the side menu.

Click Add gateway.

When prompted for the deployment type, select Operator-managed deployment. This ensures the IBM Operator handles the lifecycle, scaling, and certificate rotation for the gateway.

On the Provide details screen, configure the following settings:








Field
Configuration




Gateway group
Select Create a new gateway group and enter a name (e.g., default-group).


Gateway ID
Provide a unique identifier for this gateway (e.g., eem-gateway-lab or eem-gateway-prod).


Replicas
Leave at 1 for the lab, or scale up as needed for production.




Click Create to proceed to the Deploy Event Gateway step.
Click the copy icon on the code block to copy the generated deployment configuration and paste it into a new file named gateway-deployment.yaml.

2. Modify the Generated Configuration:
Before applying the file, you must make three important modifications:

Accept the license agreement (accept: true).
Reduce the maxNumKafkaBrokers to save cluster resources.
Define the Ingress Endpoint: The Operator requires a spec.endpoints block to know how to expose the Gateway pods to the network.

Open gateway-deployment.yaml in your text editor and modify the spec block.

Option A: Production (AWS EKS)Option B: Lab (NGINX)


Use Case: Matching the production spec on AWS EKS. We will allocate capacity for 3 brokers and define the endpoint with the ALB annotations to satisfy the webhook (though actual traffic will use our manual NLB).
# ... (inside gateway-deployment.yaml) ...
spec:
  license:
    # 1. Accept the license
    accept: true
    license: "L-CYBH-K48BZQ"
    metric: "VIRTUAL_PROCESSOR_CORE"
    use: "EventAutomationProduction"
  managerEndpoint: "https://eem.server.eem.corp/gateway"
  gatewayGroupName: "default-group"
  gatewayID: "eem-gateway-prod"
  replicas: 1
  # 2. Reduce broker capacity
  maxNumKafkaBrokers: 3
  # 3. Define the endpoint routing
    endpoints:
    - name: gateway
      host: kafka-gateway.eem.corp
      annotations:
        kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "alb"
        alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: "internal"
        alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: "ip"
  # ... rest of file remains unchanged ...


Use Case: Saving maximum resources in the k3s lab while testing the Bitnami broker. We only need 1 broker endpoint and will route it using the NGINX controller with SSL passthrough enabled.
# ... (inside gateway-deployment.yaml) ...
spec:
  license:
    # 1. Accept the license
    accept: true
    license: "L-CYBH-K48BZQ"
    metric: "VIRTUAL_PROCESSOR_CORE"
    use: "EventAutomationProduction"
  managerEndpoint: "https://eem.eem-server.gym.lan/gateway"
  gatewayGroupName: "default-group"
  gatewayID: "eem-gateway-lab"
  replicas: 1
  # 2. Reduce broker capacity
  maxNumKafkaBrokers: 1
  # 3. Define the endpoint routing
  endpoints:
    - name: gateway
      host: kafka-gateway.gym.lan
      annotations:
        kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "nginx"
        nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-passthrough: "true"
  # ... rest of file remains unchanged ...



3. Apply the Gateway CR: Once your modifications are saved, apply the YAML directly to the cluster to establish the connection:
kubectl apply -f gateway-deployment.yaml -n ibm-eem






TipVerification



Wait a few moments, then check the Gateways page in the EEM UI. Your new gateway should appear with a “Connected” status.




3.4 Expose the Gateway (Layer 4 Routing)
Because Kafka relies on strict mTLS handshakes between the client and the Gateway, standard Layer 7 HTTP/S load balancing will break the connection. We must expose the Gateway pods using a Layer 4 TCP passthrough.

Option A: AWS EKS (Manual NLB)Option B: Lab (NGINX SSL Passthrough)


Use Case: The IBM Operator generated an ALB to satisfy cluster admission webhooks, but we need an actual Network Load Balancer (NLB) to handle the TCP mTLS traffic.
Create a manual Service to provision an AWS NLB that targets the running Gateway pods directly.
Create a file named eem-gateway-nlb.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: eem-gateway-nlb
  namespace: ibm-eem
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "external"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: "ip"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internal"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-protocol: "TCP"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"
    # Anonymized enterprise tags
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-additional-resource-tags: "Name=eem-gateway-nlb,tfc-application-group=event-streaming,tfc-technical-environment=lab"
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ports:
    - name: gateway-tls
      port: 443
      targetPort: 8443
      protocol: TCP
  selector:
    # These labels target the Gateway pods provisioned by your EEM Custom Resource
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: eem-manager
    app.kubernetes.io/name: gateway
Apply the NLB Service:
kubectl apply -f eem-gateway-nlb.yaml
Update your DNS records so that gateway.eem.corp points to the new NLB hostname rather than the placeholder ALB.


Use Case: Using the in-cluster NGINX ingress controller we configured earlier.
Because we installed the NGINX controller with the --enable-ssl-passthrough=true flag, and because NGINX is an exceptionally robust choice for this kind of routing, it will automatically recognize the Gateway ingress resource and pass the raw TCP connection directly to the pods.
No additional manual services are required. Ensure your Gateway ingress resource contains this specific annotation: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-passthrough: "true"
